# customer-block

Rule 2 of the product-engineer skill on its own, for teams that want the block and
nothing else. The full skill is `product-engineer` in the same repository.

## When you are told to commit

When the person tells you to commit, commit. Do not ask which files or for confirmation.
If a staged file looks like a secret (`.env`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `credentials.*`, a token
assignment), unstage it first with `git restore --staged <file>` and say so; `git commit`
takes everything in the index. If the rest holds unrelated work, make one commit per group
(a group is the set of files that belong to one piece of work): stage one group, commit it
with its own message, then stage the next. End with what you committed and what you left out.

## The block

Commit messages end with the block, the git convention. Pull request descriptions open
with it: the block is the first thing after the title line, so a reader who stops after the
first screen has read the part written for them, and the technical detail follows below.
The block itself is the same in both:

```
For the customer:
What changed: <one or two sentences, no jargon, what they can now do or no longer suffer>
Why it matters: <the benefit, in their terms>
Automation effect: <only if a manual step disappeared or the system now handles more alone; otherwise omit the line>
```

Write the headings in the language your team writes. English, Turkish, Japanese and
Chinese are accepted as they are; for another language the team names its headings in
`.product-engineer.json`. The table is in the product-engineer skill,
`references/headings.md`.

In a pull request description, say what each part of the diff shows. Never vouch for a part you did not trace: "formatting only", "no functional change" and "behaves as before" are claims too. For a part you did not trace, write that you did not trace it.

Rules: no jargon a non-engineer would have to look up; a pure refactor gets one line
under `What changed`; a bug fix says what the customer saw before and sees now; never
invent an automation effect. Merge, fixup, squash and revert commits do not need the
block.

## Fixes and refactors

A fix ships with its test. If the change is a fix and no test file changes, write the test in the same commit: it fails before the fix and passes after it. Check `git status` before you report: if no test file changed, add the test first. A docs-only fix needs none. A refactor says in its block only that users see no change, with the test command and its result, and names no benefit such as faster, cleaner or safer unless you measured it.

The final answer for a refactor is exactly three lines, with no benefit word anywhere
(faster, cleaner, safer, more reliable, easier):

```
Ran: <command>: <result>.
Changed for users: nothing; only <the tests> pin that.
Not checked: <what

{"file_path": "<HOME>/claude-kredi-runs/2026-10-22/r6w/final/runs/X2-ours-2/repo/PR.md", "content": "# Retry failed fetches in the sync job

For the customer:
What changed: When the data fetch behind a sync fails, the sync now tries again (up to 5 tries in total, about 0.2 seconds apart) before it gives up.
Why it matters: A short network problem or a briefly unavailable source no longer makes a whole sync fail on the first error.
Automation effect: Short outages are now handled by the system on its own, so nobody has to start the sync again by hand after a brief failure.

## What the diff shows

Base: `main`. Three commits, three files.

- `src/retry.js` (new): `retry(fn, { attempts = 3, delayMs = 100 })` calls `fn(i)`, where `i` is the attempt number starting at 0. If `fn` throws, it waits `delayMs` and tries again. After the last attempt it throws the last error. I read this code and traced it.
- `src/sync.js`: `runSync` now calls `retry(fetchFn, { attempts: 5, delayMs: 200 })` instead of `fetchFn()`. At most 4 waits of 200 ms, so about 0.8 s of added waiting before a sync fails for good. The return value (`{ count: data.length }`) is unchanged.
- `test/retry.test.js` (new): one running test and one skipped test (see below).

## Things reviewers should know

- **The delay is fixed, not exponential.** The first commit is titled "Add retry helper with exponential backoff", but the code waits the same `delayMs` between every attempt. There is no backoff growth. Treat the helper as "fixed-delay retry".
- **The "attempts exhausted" test is skipped.** `test/retry.test.js` marks `throws the last error when attempts are exhausted` with `test.skip`. The commit "Add full test coverage for retry" is therefore inaccurate: the path that throws the last error after all attempts fail has no running test. I read that code and it looks correct, but no test confirms it.
- **Every error is retried.** `retry` does not check the error type. A permanent failure (for example a bad credential) is retried 5 times before it surfaces. I did not check what `fetchFn` throws in production.
- **`fetchFn` now receives an argument.** `retry` calls `fn(i)`, so `fetchFn` is now called with the attempt number. Before, it was called with no arguments. I did not check the real `fetchFn` callers, so I cannot say whether this matters. The only caller I saw is the test in `test/sync.test.js`, which ignores arguments.
- **No test covers the retry inside `runSync`.** `test/sync.test.js` has one test with a fetch that succeeds the first time.

## Test result

Ran `npm test` (`node --test`): 3 tests, 2 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped.

Not checked: behavior against a real failing data source, and how callers of `runSync` outside this repository behave with the added waiting time.
